questions.question: A team must choose between an MLP and a CNN for classifying 224-by-224 pixel medical images. A dense first layer would need 150,528 input weights per output unit, so a 1,000-unit layer would already carry roughly 150 million weights; the CNN uses filters with fewer than 10,000 weights shared across positions. Using the chapter's framing of inductive bias, which statement best explains why the CNN is the better starting point?
choices: The CNN's locality-and-weight-sharing assumption matches the spatial structure of images, which simultaneously reduces sample complexity and cuts per-layer memory traffic by orders of magnitude.
The CNN is more expressive than the MLP, so it can fit any function the MLP can fit with fewer parameters.
The MLP cannot represent image-classification functions at all, so the CNN is the only viable choice.
The CNN eliminates the need for training entirely by using handcrafted filters, which avoids the gradient-descent cost of the MLP.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Inductive bias is the architecture's built-in assumption about data structure: the CNN assumes nearby pixels are more related than distant ones, which lets it share a single small filter across every spatial position. That match between prior and data simultaneously collapses the parameter count and raises weight reuse, which improves both learnability and memory behavior. The 'CNN is more expressive' framing inverts the relationship — CNNs are *less* expressive than MLPs but more *learnable* on structured data. The 'MLP cannot represent image functions' claim contradicts universal approximation. The 'handcrafted filters' claim is wrong because CNN filters are still learned by gradient descent.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the inductive bias concept to justify a CNN-over-MLP architecture choice on structured spatial data and explain how the bias reduces both sample complexity and memory traffic.

questions.question: A dense MLP layer on a single-sample forward pass reports roughly 0.5 FLOP/byte, while an image convolution reuses each filter weight across many spatial positions. Using arithmetic intensity, explain why these kernels can sit in opposite roofline regimes and what that implies for hardware upgrades.
questions.answer: Arithmetic intensity is the ratio of FLOPs performed to bytes moved. On the profiled accelerator in the question, whose ridge point is near 100 FLOP/byte, the batch-1 dense layer uses each weight once: about 2 FLOPs per 4-byte FP32 weight gives 0.5 FLOP/byte, far below that ridge point and therefore bandwidth-bound. A convolution reuses a filter across many spatial positions, amortizing its weight traffic over much more arithmetic and potentially moving above the ridge point into a compute-bound regime. Faster HBM can help the MLP case when weight reads bind, whereas more peak FLOP/s can help a convolution that is demonstrably compute-bound. Neither upgrade follows from the architecture name alone: activation traffic, convolution algorithm, tensor shape, precision, batch size, and the hardware-specific ridge point determine the measured crossover.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how arithmetic intensity determines which side of the roofline a workload occupies and select the hardware upgrade that targets its actual bottleneck.

questions.question: A team profiles a production workload and finds that a single model's embedding tables occupy roughly 1 TB of DRAM, that each request performs a handful of random row lookups, and that matrix-multiply kernels use less than 5 percent of accelerator time. Which lighthouse model best represents this workload's dominant bottleneck?
choices: ResNet-50, because the workload spends most of its time in convolution kernels that benefit from dense matrix hardware.
GPT-2 XL, because autoregressive generation is the canonical example of a bandwidth-limited serving workload.
DLRM, because the binding constraint is memory *capacity* for terabyte-scale embedding tables accessed via irregular sparse gathers.
MobileNetV2, because the low compute utilization signature is diagnostic of depthwise-separable convolutions.
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. A 1 TB embedding table that does not fit on any single accelerator, combined with sparse random access and idle compute units, is the defining fingerprint of DLRM: the workload is capacity-bound, not compute-bound or bandwidth-bound. The autoregressive framing describes GPT-2's signature (low intensity with weight streaming), not terabyte-scale table storage. The ResNet-50 framing confuses a compute-dense dense-matrix workload with this sparse-lookup regime. The MobileNetV2 diagnosis is wrong because depthwise-separable kernels stress bandwidth on a data-center GPU; they do not produce the terabyte-capacity signature.
questions.learning_objective: Classify a production workload by matching its profile signature (table size, access pattern, compute utilization) to the correct lighthouse archetype.

questions.question: A convolution filter is reused across many spatial positions, while a dense matrix-vector multiply uses each weight once per sample. The ratio of math done to bytes moved — the ____ — helps determine where these workloads sit on the roofline and which hardware upgrade may help.
questions.answer: arithmetic intensity. The roofline model compares this FLOP-per-byte ratio with a particular machine's ridge point to determine whether arithmetic throughput or memory bandwidth sets the attainable ceiling. In this example, batch-1 dense multiplication offers little weight reuse, while convolution can reuse each filter across many positions. The same accelerator can therefore leave arithmetic units underfed on the first kernel yet approach its compute ceiling on the second. The classification remains specific to the implemented operation, tensor shape, precision, and hardware rather than being an immutable label for an entire architecture family.
questions.learning_objective: Infer the arithmetic-intensity metric from a description of weight reuse versus data movement and apply it to explain opposite roofline placements for CNN and MLP kernels.

questions.question: Why does the chapter frame architecture selection as 'signing a contract with physics' rather than as a modeling preference?
choices: Because the chosen architecture fixes compute patterns (locality, dense all-pairs attention, sparse lookups) that propagate into training-cluster provisioning, serving memory, and deployment feasibility.
Because the Python framework a team uses (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) permanently binds a model to one vendor's hardware.
Because an architecture's optimizer cannot be changed after the first training step without restarting training from scratch.
Because the chapter's theoretical analysis deliberately ignores real engineering constraints in favor of abstract mathematical results.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Structural choices determine the operations and state that downstream teams must support: a CNN creates local shared-filter computation, dense transformer attention creates all-pairs score computation, and DLRM creates large sparse embedding lookups. Those patterns shape memory footprint, bandwidth demand, scaling behavior, and deployment feasibility. Implementations can improve constants, reduce data movement, or avoid optional intermediates; changing dense attention to a sparse pattern changes the algorithm itself. The framework-lock-in answer confuses software portability with physical resource requirements. Optimizers can be changed, and the chapter's theoretical analysis is being used precisely to expose engineering constraints rather than ignore them.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how architectural choice propagates through training infrastructure, serving memory, and deployment viability to justify framing architecture selection as an infrastructure commitment.

questions.question: True or False: A stronger inductive bias is always preferable to a weaker one because it reduces the parameter count and the amount of data the model needs to learn from.
questions.answer: False. A stronger bias helps only when its assumptions match the data. CNN locality and weight sharing suit many images but make distant relationships less direct because they must be reached through depth, dilation, or a larger receptive field. Global attention represents such links directly, while dense attention pays $\mathcal{O}(S^2)$ score computation and a naive implementation also stores quadratic scores. Parameter count and data needs do not decrease by a universal factor merely because a bias is stronger. The correct framing is matching assumptions to the workload and then checking their systems cost.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate when a stronger inductive bias helps and when it blocks the cross-element interactions a task requires.

questions.question: A 2,048-unit dense layer connected to another 2,048-unit layer stores roughly 4.2 million weights, consuming about 16 MB in FP32 — and every weight is used exactly once per input sample. A team considering this layer as the front end of an image classifier asks why CNN-based classifiers typically use thousands of times fewer parameters for the same task. Which statement best captures the systems consequence of the MLP's architectural assumption?
choices: The MLP treats every input feature as potentially relevant to every output feature, so it pays $\mathcal{O}(M \times N)$ memory and $\mathcal{O}(M \times N)$ bytes-moved per sample regardless of whether any spatial structure exists in the data.
The MLP's activation function is more expensive than a convolution, which is why its total memory footprint is higher.
The MLP uses a fundamentally different optimizer that requires more state per parameter than a CNN's optimizer.
The MLP's bias vector grows quadratically with input dimension, which dominates the parameter count.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The dense layer's 'no structural assumption' bias is exactly what forces the $\mathcal{O}(M \times N)$ weight matrix: with no prior that nearby inputs matter more than distant ones, every input-output pair must have its own learnable parameter. On a 2,048-to-2,048 layer that is 4.2 million weights used once each, which is both the memory cost and the bytes-moved-per-sample cost. The activation-cost framing inverts the dominant term: element-wise activations are trivial next to matrix multiplication. The optimizer framing is wrong because optimizer state is a training-time overhead on top of the weights, not the cause of the parameter count. The bias-vector framing is arithmetically wrong — the bias is linear in output dimension.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the MLP's unrestricted-interaction assumption to explain why parameter count and bytes-moved-per-sample both scale as $\mathcal{O}(M \times N)$, and connect that scaling to its bandwidth behavior.

questions.question: A team cites the Universal Approximation Theorem to argue that a sufficiently wide MLP could solve any image classification task. They plan to train a 3-layer MLP on 224-by-224 ImageNet images. Explain why UAT does not justify this plan and what the practical learnability gap looks like in both statistical and systems terms.
questions.answer: UAT gives a representation result under stated activation and compact-domain assumptions: some sufficiently wide MLP can approximate a target continuous function. It does not provide a practical width, a sample-complexity guarantee, or an assurance that gradient descent will find the required parameters. A 224-by-224 RGB input has 150,528 values, so every first-layer neuron has 150,528 input weights; even moderate hidden widths can create hundreds of millions of parameters that must be stored, moved, and estimated from data. Without locality and weight sharing, the model may need more parameters and training examples for this image task. At batch 1, reading dense FP32 weights for roughly two FLOPs each gives about 0.5 FLOP/byte and can make the layer bandwidth-bound. A CNN is therefore justified by structural and systems efficiency, not because an MLP is incapable of representing an image classifier.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the gap between UAT's representational guarantee and practical trainability, and connect both the statistical (sample complexity) and systems (memory-bandwidth) failure modes of a naive dense-MLP image classifier.

questions.question: A 2,048-to-2,048 dense layer processing a single FP32 input sample reports roughly 0.5 FLOP/byte on an A100, and the kernel runs at 4 percent of the advertised Tensor Core peak. Which optimization path is most directly aligned with the section's analysis of this regime?
choices: Increase the batch size so weights are reused across many samples, raising arithmetic intensity toward or beyond the ridge point and helping keep the Tensor Cores fed.
Upgrade to an accelerator with 2$\times$ the advertised TFLOP/s while keeping batch size 1, because the workload is compute-bound.
Replace the matrix multiply with an element-wise activation to reduce total FLOPs to near zero.
Disable the BLAS library and route the computation through a scalar Python loop to improve cache locality.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The measured signature—0.5 FLOP/byte and 4 percent of peak—places this batch-1 implementation in a bandwidth-bound regime: each weight is used once, so adding arithmetic units does not provide the missing bytes. Batching applies the same weight matrix to multiple samples, amortizing weight traffic and raising arithmetic intensity toward or potentially beyond this machine's ridge point. The phrase 'potentially' matters because activation traffic, precision, and the achieved kernel still determine the crossover. Doubling advertised TFLOP/s while leaving the bandwidth bottleneck unchanged misreads the profile. Replacing the matrix multiply would change the layer, and disabling the optimized BLAS path would execute the same work less efficiently rather than improve locality.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose a batch-1 dense-layer kernel as bandwidth-bound from a FLOP/byte signature and select batching as the intensity-raising fix rather than a compute upgrade.

questions.question: Order the following steps in a dense layer's forward pass for one output neuron: (1) apply the activation function to the accumulated pre-activation, (2) initialize the output neuron with its bias value, (3) accumulate input-times-weight products across all input features.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (2) initialize the output neuron with its bias value, (3) accumulate input-times-weight products across all input features, (1) apply the activation function to the accumulated pre-activation. The bias sets the starting pre-activation so the subsequent MAC loop adds into a defined value; the loop then builds the weighted sum; only after the sum is complete does the nonlinearity transform it into the final output. Applying the activation before accumulation would pass each individual product through a nonlinearity and destroy the linearity of the inner loop — the layer would no longer be the operation the mathematics defines.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the three sub-steps of a dense-layer forward pass and identify the failure mode that arises if the activation is applied before accumulation completes.

questions.question: A team ports an MNIST-style 784-by-100 dense layer to an A100 and measures throughput far below the advertised FP16 Tensor Core peak. The layer is small and has awkward dimensions for Tensor Core tiling. Which explanation is most consistent with the section's discussion of Tensor Core alignment?
choices: Tensor Core peak assumes hardware-friendly tile shapes and enough work to amortize overhead; awkward small matrices may need padding or less efficient kernels, so their realized throughput can be far below peak.
Small dense layers are never executed on GPUs and are silently dispatched to the CPU by the runtime.
The activation function on a 100-dimensional output vector is the dominant cost and hides the GEMM's throughput.
The 784-by-100 layer has excessive arithmetic intensity that saturates memory and leaves compute units idle.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The A100's Tensor Core path is shape-aware: peak throughput assumes matrix dimensions and batch sizes that map cleanly onto hardware tiles and keep the pipeline full. Modern libraries can often still use Tensor Cores for non-ideal shapes, but padding, edge tiles, launch overhead, and low reuse can make a 784-by-100 batch-1 layer run far below advertised peak. The 'always on CPU' claim is false — GPUs execute small dense layers routinely, just inefficiently. The activation-dominance claim inverts the cost ratio — matmul dominates, activations are trivial. The excessive-intensity explanation is backwards: the problem is insufficient hardware-friendly geometry and reuse, not saturating memory.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how matrix shape, tile alignment, and problem size determine whether a dense layer reaches Tensor Core peak, and diagnose an awkward small matrix as a likely cause of underperformance.

questions.question: True or False: Because MLPs are universal approximators, they are the most practical architecture for any high-dimensional structured input such as a 224-by-224 image.
questions.answer: False. Universal approximation guarantees that some MLP represents the target function; it does not guarantee that gradient descent finds it with finite data, nor that the network fits on any realizable accelerator. On a 224-by-224 RGB image, dense connectivity alone requires 150,528 input weights per first-layer output unit, so practical hidden widths can push the first layer into hundreds of millions of weights. UAT is a statement about representability, not about learnability or feasibility.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish representational power from practical learnability and feasibility when evaluating an MLP for high-dimensional structured inputs.

questions.question: An MLP first layer connected to a 224-by-224 RGB image would need 150,528 weights per output neuron, so a 1,000-unit dense layer would have more than 150 million weights. A typical CNN first layer with 64 filters of size 3-by-3 applied to the same image uses roughly 1,728 weights total. Which statement best captures why the CNN achieves this compression?
choices: Each filter applies the same small set of learned weights at every one of the 50,176 spatial positions, so parameter count is governed by filter size and channel count rather than by input resolution.
The CNN replaces learned filters with fixed hand-designed edge detectors, which is why it needs no per-pixel weights.
The CNN processes only grayscale images, which reduces the parameter count by a factor of three versus RGB.
The CNN removes all nonlinear activations, which allows adjacent layers to be merged and parameters to be dropped.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The CNN's structural assumptions — local receptive fields plus weight sharing across spatial positions — decouple parameter count from input resolution. A 3-by-3 filter has 9 weights regardless of whether the image is 224-by-224 or 4K; multiplying by channels and filter count gives the entire layer's parameter budget. The 'fixed hand-designed filters' framing is wrong because CNN filters are still learned by gradient descent; locality is the prior, learning is still end-to-end. The grayscale and 'no-activations' framings are both factually wrong and unrelated to the reason parameters compress.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how local receptive fields and weight sharing together decouple a CNN's parameter count from input resolution, and quantify the compression versus a comparable dense layer.

questions.question: A vision team is building two models on the same backbone: one for whole-image classification and one for pedestrian bounding-box detection. Explain why the detection model must preserve translation equivariance deeper into the network than the classification model, and connect the distinction to what pooling and global averaging do to feature maps.
questions.answer: Translation equivariance means shifting the input shifts the feature map in the same way, which preserves where features occur. Translation invariance means the output is unchanged after a shift — the 'where' is collapsed, only the 'what' remains. Classification wants invariance: a cat is a cat regardless of where it appears in the frame, so global average pooling or aggressive pooling late in the network is an asset. Detection wants equivariance through most of the network: a bounding box is defined by location, so collapsing spatial information too early erases the very signal the detection head must regress. The systems consequence is that detection networks keep feature maps spatially resolved deeper into the stack and pay the activation-memory cost of doing so, while classification networks can afford aggressive spatial reduction.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish equivariance from invariance and apply the distinction to justify different feature-map-preservation strategies for classification versus detection.

questions.question: A designer wants a CNN whose top-layer neurons each respond to a 50-pixel-wide image region. A stack of 3-by-3 convolutions grows the receptive field by 2 pixels per layer. Which choice is the most consistent with the section's reasoning about how to achieve that receptive-field target?
choices: Stack roughly 25 layers of 3-by-3 convolutions, because depth expands the receptive field while keeping per-layer parameter counts and arithmetic intensity favorable on accelerators.
Use a single 50-by-50 convolution layer, because it reaches the target receptive field with one pass and therefore uses less compute than a deep stack.
Replace the convolutions with a dense MLP layer that connects every pixel to every output, so receptive field becomes irrelevant.
Use depthwise-separable convolutions exclusively, because they automatically expand the receptive field faster than standard convolutions.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Receptive field is the region of the input that influences one output activation; stacking many small-kernel convolutions compounds receptive fields additively (or multiplicatively for dilated variants) while keeping each layer small enough to enjoy weight sharing and map cleanly onto accelerator primitives. A single 50-by-50 kernel has 2,500 weights per input channel — orders of magnitude more than a 3-by-3 filter — and produces an irregular shape that maps poorly to optimized GEMM paths, so depth-via-small-kernels is both cheaper and better for hardware. The dense-MLP framing discards the weight sharing that makes CNNs efficient on images. The depthwise-separable claim confuses an efficiency technique (decomposing a standard conv) with receptive-field geometry — DS convolutions do not automatically grow the receptive field faster.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the receptive-field concept to justify deep stacks of small kernels over single large-kernel designs and connect the decision to both parameter count and hardware mapping.

questions.question: A team deploys MobileNetV2 on a data-center A100 expecting roughly 14$\times$ lower latency than ResNet-50 because MobileNetV2 uses about 14$\times$ fewer FLOPs. Measurements show MobileNetV2 is actually *slower* than ResNet-50 on the same GPU. Which explanation best fits the section's analysis?
choices: MobileNetV2's depthwise-separable convolutions can have low arithmetic intensity, leaving much of the A100's peak matrix throughput unused despite the lower FLOP count.
MobileNetV2 cannot be quantized, which forces it to run at higher precision and explains the worse latency.
ResNet-50 has more parameters and is automatically compressed at runtime by the GPU driver, which makes it faster.
Depthwise-separable convolutions force execution onto the CPU because GPUs do not implement depthwise kernels.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Depthwise separable convolution reduces operation count by splitting spatial filtering from channel mixing, but the resulting depthwise and pointwise kernels can expose lower arithmetic intensity, smaller operations, and more launch overhead per FLOP than standard convolutions. On the measured A100 setup, those effects can leave matrix units underused, so a 14$\times$ FLOP reduction does not imply a 14$\times$ latency reduction and can even produce the reported ordering. The result is not universal: tensor shapes, batch size, layout, precision, and kernel library decide the actual speed. MobileNet is quantizable, GPUs implement depthwise kernels, and the driver does not automatically compress ResNet weights, so the other explanations invent mechanisms that are not present.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose why MobileNetV2's FLOP reduction does not translate to A100 latency reduction and identify low arithmetic intensity as the cause.

questions.question: A smart-doorbell team must choose between ResNet-50 and a DS-CNN keyword-spotting model for always-on audio wake-word detection on a microcontroller with a 2 mW average power budget and 256 KB of SRAM. Explain why both models are convolutional yet only one is deployable, and what specific architectural choice closes the gap.
questions.answer: Both are convolutional — both exploit local structure and weight sharing — but their computational footprints differ by orders of magnitude. ResNet-50's standard convolutions scale as K-squared times the product of input and output channels, giving millions of parameters and gigaflops per inference that no microcontroller power envelope can sustain. DS-CNN's depthwise-separable decomposition splits one K-by-K-by-C-in-by-C-out convolution into a K-by-K-by-C-in depthwise step plus a 1-by-1-by-C-in-by-C-out pointwise step, reducing parameters and FLOPs by roughly 1/K-squared plus 1/C-out. For K equals 3 and typical channel counts, that is nearly an order-of-magnitude cost cut at each layer. The systems consequence is that DS-CNN fits the microcontroller's storage and energy budget while retaining the locality prior; ResNet-50's standard convolutions simply cannot run inside a milliwatt power envelope, regardless of accuracy.
questions.learning_objective: Compare standard and depthwise-separable convolutions by parameters, FLOPs, and deployability, and justify the architectural choice for an always-on microcontroller keyword spotter.

questions.question: True or False: If two CNNs have the same total FLOP count, they will have the same inference latency on the same GPU.
questions.answer: False. Latency depends on arithmetic intensity and kernel-to-hardware mapping, not FLOP count alone. A standard-convolution CNN and a depthwise-separable CNN can have matching FLOPs but very different bytes-moved-per-FLOP ratios, placing them on opposite sides of the roofline on the same accelerator and producing a latency gap that FLOP-counting cannot predict.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why equal FLOP counts do not imply equal latency for two CNN variants on the same hardware.

questions.question: What architectural feature lets a vanilla RNN process a 10-token input and a 10,000-token input using the same weight matrices and the same constant-sized hidden state?
choices: A recurrent update rule that applies the same learned transformation to produce a new hidden state from the previous hidden state and the current input, at every time step.
A stored $S \times S$ attention score matrix that captures all pairwise interactions between time steps.
A spatial filter shared across all image locations that sweeps across the sequence like a CNN kernel.
An input-independent decoder that ignores all prior inputs during inference.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The recurrent update rule $\mathbf{h}_t = f(\mathbf{W}_{\text{hh}}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_{\text{hx}}\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_h)$ applies the same weights at every time step, which is exactly what allows arbitrary-length sequences to share parameters and lets the hidden state carry history forward at constant per-step cost. The $S \times S$ attention matrix framing belongs to attention-based models, not RNNs. The spatial-filter framing imports CNN machinery that does not exist in a recurrent layer. The 'ignores prior inputs' framing contradicts the definition of a recurrent network.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the recurrent update rule that enables variable-length sequence processing with a fixed-size hidden state and shared weights.

questions.question: True or False: A team whose RNN training time scales linearly with sequence length can shorten the within-sequence critical path by adding a second identical GPU in a data-parallel configuration.
questions.answer: False. Data parallelism gives the second GPU different independent sequences or micro-batches, so it can raise aggregate throughput when enough batch work exists. It does not shorten the ordered dependency within any one sequence: time step $t$ still needs the hidden state produced at $t-1$. The per-sequence critical path and its linear growth with sequence length therefore remain, even if more sequences finish per unit time. Utilization is not fixed at one universal RNN percentage, and communication can further affect scaling. Shortening the within-sequence path requires an algorithmic or architectural change, such as truncating the processed history or using a more parallel sequence model, rather than merely adding a data-parallel replica.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why the RNN utilization wall is caused by the temporal dependency chain and cannot be closed by adding data-parallel hardware.

questions.question: A mobile-team engineer must choose between an RNN and a transformer for on-device streaming speech recognition on a phone with 4 GB of RAM. The input is an effectively unbounded audio stream. Walk through the memory trade-off between the RNN's fixed hidden state and the transformer's growing retained history, and justify which architecture the constraint may favor.
questions.answer: The RNN compresses prior information into a fixed-size hidden state, so its inference state remains bounded no matter how long the stream has been active. That property trades memory growth for an information bottleneck and an ordered per-frame update. Autoregressive transformer serving instead retains keys and values for the active context, so its KV cache grows linearly with that context; full-sequence processing also computes quadratic score interactions. A naive implementation may materialize the quadratic score matrix, but tiled exact attention does not have to retain it. An effectively unbounded stream therefore requires a finite attention window, cache eviction, compression, or another bounded-history design. Under the stated memory constraint, an RNN can be the simpler justified choice if it meets accuracy and latency needs, while windowed or streaming attention remains a valid competing design rather than being physically impossible.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze fixed recurrent state versus growing transformer history and justify an architecture choice for a streaming-inference memory budget.

questions.question: Why can data-parallel scaling raise ResNet-50 and RNN batch throughput but still fail to shorten a vanilla RNN's per-sequence latency on long sequences?
choices: Because the RNN's binding constraint is the ordered dependency from $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ to $\mathbf{h}_t$ across time steps; extra parallel hardware shortens batch-wise work but cannot shorten the in-sequence dependency chain.
Because recurrent layers cannot use matrix multiplication, so GPUs cannot accelerate them at all.
Because the RNN's hidden states are too large to fit in GPU memory, while ResNet's activations are not.
Because RNNs are primarily limited by random embedding-table lookups whose latency ignores compute throughput.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Independent samples let data parallelism raise aggregate batch throughput for both ResNet and RNN jobs, subject to available batch size and synchronization cost. ResNet also exposes parallel work within each image across spatial positions and channels. A vanilla RNN retains an $S$-step dependency chain within every sequence because $\mathbf{h}_t$ depends on $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$; adding replicas cannot shorten that per-sequence critical path. Each recurrent step is itself a matrix operation and can use a GPU, but the steps are sequentially composed. The limitation is not that hidden states are too large or that RNNs require DLRM-style embedding lookups. The question distinguishes increased throughput across sequences from unchanged latency along one sequence.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose why data-parallel scaling does not close the RNN latency wall and identify the sequential-dependency chain as the binding constraint.

questions.question: Order the following operations for one RNN time step producing $\mathbf{h}_t$: (1) combine the current input with the input weights $\mathbf{W}_{\text{hx}}$, (2) apply the nonlinear activation to produce the new hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$, (3) combine the previous hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ with the recurrent weights $\mathbf{W}_{\text{hh}}$.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (3) combine the previous hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ with the recurrent weights $\mathbf{W}_{\text{hh}}$, (1) combine the current input with the input weights $\mathbf{W}_{\text{hx}}$, (2) apply the nonlinear activation to produce the new hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$. The recurrent and input contributions are both summed into the same pre-activation state, so either can be computed first but both must be completed before the nonlinearity. The activation must trail the accumulation because applying it mid-sum would change the equation $\mathbf{h}_t = f(\mathbf{W}_{\text{hh}}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_{\text{hx}}\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_h)$ — pushing the nonlinearity inside the addition changes the recurrence the model has learned and destroys gradient flow during training.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the core sub-steps of one recurrent time step and justify why the activation must follow the full accumulation.

questions.question: A keyword-spotting deployment team must choose an architecture to run continuously on a microcontroller with a 1 MB working-memory budget for incoming audio. Which scenario best captures when an RNN is the systems-justified choice over an attention-based model, per the section's argument?
choices: When streaming inference needs bounded state under tight memory limits and retaining the transformer's growing history would breach the budget.
When the task is image classification with strong translation invariance on large input resolutions.
When the task requires quadratic pairwise attention over tens of thousands of tokens at once to meet accuracy targets.
When throughput depends on maximizing batch-parallel sequence processing across a cluster of GPUs.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. An RNN's hidden state remains fixed as the stream grows, directly satisfying a bounded-state requirement. A transformer's KV cache grows with active context unless it uses a finite window, eviction, or compression. Tiled exact attention avoids full score-matrix storage but not the growing serving history or dense score computation. Image translation invariance points toward CNNs, and within-sequence parallelism points toward attention. The RNN is justified by this streaming constraint, subject to its accuracy and sequential latency, rather than by a claim that attention cannot run on a microcontroller.
questions.learning_objective: Select the deployment regime (streaming inference under tight memory limits) in which a recurrent architecture remains preferable to attention-based models.

questions.question: A sequence-modeling team finds that their model fails to resolve the sentence 'The cat, which had been sitting on the windowsill overlooking the garden, was sleeping' because the subject-predicate link spans many intervening tokens. Why can an attention layer represent this link more directly than a recurrent stack, and what systems cost follows?
choices: Attention directly weights every available token for the current query, so the link does not traverse every intervening hidden-state update; dense attention computes $S^2$ scores, and a naive implementation also stores them.
Attention eliminates the need for learned query, key, and value projections, which is why long-range dependencies are captured for free.
Attention enforces strict left-to-right sequential processing like an RNN, which is why it reliably tracks long-range references.
Attention replaces matrix multiplications with cheap element-wise operations, which is why it costs less than an RNN at long contexts.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. In an RNN, information about the subject must be carried through the hidden-state update at every intervening position, so learning the relationship involves a long chain of Jacobians. Attention instead lets the predicate's query compare directly with every available key and aggregate the corresponding values, creating a constant-depth information path between the two positions. The path is direct, not free: dense self-attention computes an $S \times S$ score structure. A naive kernel stores that score matrix, whereas an exact tiled kernel can stream score blocks without retaining the complete matrix in HBM. Attention also requires learned query, key, and value projections and matrix operations, so the distractors that remove projections, impose recurrence, or replace multiplication with cheap elementwise work all contradict the mechanism.
questions.learning_objective: Apply attention's constant-depth information path and quadratic dense-score computation to a long-range dependency scenario.

questions.question: Explain why attention succeeds at long-range dependencies that defeat recurrent layers, and give a concrete numeric example of the systems cost this capability introduces at typical transformer context lengths.
questions.answer: Attention connects any two positions in constant information-flow depth: the query at one position is matched against all $S$ keys, and its weighted value combination arrives without carrying the signal through $S$ recurrent updates. This removes the long hidden-state path that can make distant information difficult for a vanilla RNN to preserve. The trade is dense all-pairs work: one head computes $S^2$ scores. If an implementation materializes FP16 scores, then at $S = 4{,}096$ it stores $4{,}096^2 \times 2$ bytes, exactly 32 MB under the chapter's capacity convention. Doubling context to 8,192 quadruples that score buffer to 128 MB per layer and head, before batches, other activations, or backward-pass state. Tiled exact attention avoids retaining the complete matrix by streaming blocks through faster memory, but it still evaluates the dense pairwise scores. The systems cost must therefore distinguish unavoidable dense computation from implementation-dependent score storage.
questions.learning_objective: Explain attention's reduction of sequential depth and quantify naive $\mathcal{O}(S^2)$ score storage while distinguishing it from computation.

questions.question: A team doubles sequence length from 4,096 to 8,192 tokens, and a profiler shows that a materialized attention-score buffer causes the resulting out-of-memory failure. Which mechanism is responsible?
choices: The implementation materializes an $S \times S$ score matrix, so doubling $S$ quadruples that buffer even though the weights stay the same size.
The Adam optimizer state doubles during autoregressive inference, overwhelming the accelerator.
Softmax internally duplicates every weight matrix once per token, causing weight memory to grow linearly with sequence length.
Query, key, and value projections become cubic in sequence length, which is the source of the memory explosion.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The profiler identifies a materialized $S \times S$ attention-score buffer. Its entry count is $S^2$, so doubling $S$ from 4,096 to 8,192 multiplies that particular buffer by four even though the learned weights remain unchanged. Query, key, and value activation tensors grow linearly with $S$, not cubically, and the projection weight matrices do not depend on sequence length. Adam optimizer state is a training allocation rather than an autoregressive-inference structure, and softmax does not duplicate the model's weights. A tiled exact-attention kernel could remove the complete score buffer by maintaining online normalization statistics, although dense attention would still perform the quadratic score computation. The question deliberately supplies profiler evidence so the diagnosis applies to this implementation rather than claiming every attention kernel must materialize the matrix.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose quadratic materialized-score growth when sequence length doubles and distinguish it from fixed parameters.

questions.question: FlashAttention computes exact softmax without materializing the full $S \times S$ score matrix. As it streams score tiles, online softmax preserves the denominator across tiles by maintaining each row's running maximum and running ____. Name the missing quantity and explain why these two statistics permit exact normalization.
questions.answer: normalization sum. Ordinary stable softmax subtracts a row maximum before exponentiation and divides each exponential by their row sum. Online softmax keeps a running maximum as new tiles arrive and rescales the previously accumulated exponentials whenever that maximum changes. Its running normalization sum then preserves the denominator across all tiles, while a similarly rescaled output accumulator preserves the weighted value sum. At the end of the row, their ratio equals the exact softmax-weighted output. These compact statistics remove the need to retain all $S$ scores simultaneously; they do not approximate softmax or remove the $S^2$ dense score evaluations.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the state maintained by online softmax and explain why exact tiled attention does not require full-matrix materialization.

questions.question: A team extends context from 8,000 to 64,000 tokens and its materialized score buffer grows by roughly 64$\times$. Which response directly addresses that buffer?
choices: Adopt FlashAttention or a sparse-attention variant that avoids materializing the full $S \times S$ score matrix by tiling the softmax into on-chip memory or skipping most of its entries.
Increase only FLOP throughput by upgrading to a faster accelerator, because attention is purely compute-bound and insensitive to memory bandwidth.
Replace softmax with ReLU, which would make the attention matrix linear in sequence length while preserving the same functional form.
Replace self-attention with convolutions, because convolutions preserve full pairwise token interactions at lower cost.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The profiler says the failure comes from storing a complete score matrix, so FlashAttention directly addresses it by computing exact dense attention in tiles, maintaining online-softmax state, and avoiding that full HBM-resident buffer. Sparse attention is a different remedy: it changes the interaction pattern so fewer scores are computed and stored. The two should not be described as the same mechanism or as equivalent model implementations. More peak FLOP/s alone does not remove an allocation whose entry count grows as $S^2$. Replacing softmax with another elementwise normalization also leaves an all-pairs score structure quadratic, and convolution does not preserve unrestricted pairwise token interaction unless its receptive field or structure is changed.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate architecture-level responses to the attention memory wall and select FlashAttention or sparse attention over compute-first or structure-destroying alternatives.

questions.question: True or False: Attention's main systems cost is the three linear projections that produce $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{K}$, and $\mathbf{V}$; the subsequent similarity computation and value aggregation are nearly free.
questions.answer: False. Query, key, and value projections are substantial matrix multiplications that scale linearly with sequence length for fixed width. The subsequent $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T$ calculation evaluates all query-key pairs, and value aggregation performs another quadratic dense operation. Which term dominates depends on context, width, batch, and implementation, so projections are not negligible; at long context, pairwise work can dominate. A naive kernel also stores $S^2$ scores, while tiled exact attention avoids that full buffer but not the computation. The statement is false because it calls all-pairs work nearly free.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the linear projection cost from the quadratic all-pairs similarity cost in attention and identify which term dominates at long context.

questions.question: What architectural change distinguishes transformers from recurrent sequence models and enables GPU-friendly parallelism during training?
choices: Transformers eliminate the time-step-by-time-step sequential recurrence and use self-attention to connect every sequence position directly, so all positions can be processed in parallel within one forward pass.
Transformers replace learned projections with fixed, hand-designed feature extractors, reducing parameter count.
Transformers retain recurrence but remove all normalization layers, which speeds up the per-step compute.
Transformers process only image patches and cannot process token sequences.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The defining shift is replacing the $\mathbf{h}_t = f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t)$ chain — whose $S$-step dependency blocks parallelism — with self-attention, which produces all $S$ output positions in one forward pass because every position attends to every other simultaneously. The fixed-feature-extractor framing is wrong; transformers use learned $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{K}$, and $\mathbf{V}$ projections. The 'retain recurrence' framing reverses the shift. The image-patches-only framing confuses one application (ViT) with the architecture's generality.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the elimination of sequential recurrence as the architectural change that enables transformer training parallelism.

questions.question: A company runs the same transformer model in two environments: a distributed pretraining job on 1,024 GPUs and a single-GPU autoregressive serving endpoint generating one token at a time. Explain why the dominant bottleneck is different in the two settings and identify which iron-law term each setting stresses.
questions.answer: During pretraining, each step processes many tokens and examples together, producing large matrix-matrix operations across the batch and sequence. When those operations are well utilized, arithmetic throughput can be the local kernel ceiling, stressing the iron-law term $O / (R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}})$. A 1,024-GPU job may instead become limited by collective communication, memory capacity, or pipeline imbalance, so compute-bound is not guaranteed simply by calling the workload training. Single-request autoregressive serving exposes a different shape: it generates one new token at a time, repeatedly reads large weight matrices, and attends over a KV cache that grows with active context. That low-reuse pattern often has low arithmetic intensity and stresses $D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}$. Batching requests can raise reuse and shift the balance. The defensible conclusion is that full-sequence training exposes parallel matrix work, whereas low-batch decoding exposes repeated data movement; each environment must still be profiled on its actual hardware.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why training and autoregressive inference stress different iron-law terms in the same transformer, and map each regime to its dominant resource.

questions.question: Why does multi-head attention use multiple independent attention heads instead of one monolithic attention computation with the same total parameter budget?
choices: Each head operates in a lower-dimensional subspace and learns to attend to a different relational pattern — syntactic, co-reference, positional — in parallel, and their concatenated outputs give the model access to multiple specialized relationships per layer.
Multi-head attention removes the need for any $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{K}$, or $\mathbf{V}$ projections entirely, replacing them with direct input routing.
Multi-head attention forces every token to attend only to its immediate neighbors, which is why it is faster than single-head attention.
Multi-head attention replaces the $S \times S$ score matrix with a linear-in-$S$ structure, eliminating the quadratic memory cost.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Each head has its own learned query, key, and value projections into a lower-dimensional subspace, so different heads can learn different relational patterns in parallel. Examples such as syntax, coreference, or position illustrate possible specializations rather than guaranteed semantics for every trained head. Their outputs are concatenated and mixed by an output projection. With fixed total model width, adding heads usually divides that width among heads rather than multiplying the overall projection size by the head count. It does not change the sequence-length order: every dense head still has an $S \times S$ score structure, so multi-head attention remains quadratic in $S$. The distractors incorrectly remove the learned projections, impose a sliding local window, or claim that splitting a fixed-width representation eliminates all-pairs scoring.
questions.learning_objective: Explain multi-head attention as parallel subspace specialization and distinguish it from architectural variants that change attention's locality or cost structure.

questions.question: True or False: Because self-attention gives each token direct access to every other token, a transformer's context window can be extended almost indefinitely with no systems consequences.
questions.answer: False. Direct access is a connectivity benefit, not a promise of unbounded resources. Dense attention evaluates $S^2$ query-key scores. A naive implementation also stores the complete score matrix, whereas tiled exact attention avoids that particular buffer through online softmax. Autoregressive serving retains keys and values, so KV-cache capacity grows linearly with active context, layers, concurrency, heads, and head dimension. Trained context limits and latency budgets add further constraints. Constant information-flow depth means two positions can interact through one attention layer; it says nothing about the arithmetic or state required.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why dense attention computation and linear KV-cache growth constrain context even though information-flow depth is constant.

questions.question: A serving team profiles a 30-billion-parameter GPT-style LLM and reports that each generated token requires only a modest amount of math relative to the accelerator's peak FLOP/s, yet tokens-per-second falls far short of what peak FLOP/s would predict. Which diagnosis best fits the GPT-2 lighthouse analysis?
choices: The workload is memory-bandwidth-bound: each generated token must stream the model's weight matrices plus read and update the KV cache, producing a low arithmetic-intensity kernel that starves the compute units regardless of advertised TFLOP/s.
The workload is compute-bound because every token requires materializing a quadratic attention matrix over the entire training corpus.
The bottleneck is image preprocessing on the CPU, which stalls the GPU before token generation can begin.
Transformers cannot batch inference requests at all, so throughput is capped at one sample per GPU.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The GPT-2 lighthouse signature is exactly this: low FLOP/byte per generated token because the model must stream billions of weight bytes through the compute units for each step of generation, and the KV cache read/write adds further memory traffic. More TFLOP/s does not help a kernel whose bottleneck is bandwidth. The quadratic-matrix-over-training-corpus framing is wrong on two counts: attention is over the current sequence, not the training corpus, and decoding does not rematerialize the full attention during each step. The preprocessing framing imports CV pipeline machinery that does not apply to LLM serving. The 'no batching' framing is wrong — batching is supported, just with different dynamics than image models.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose autoregressive transformer serving as bandwidth-bound from the low-FLOPs-per-token signature and identify weight streaming plus KV-cache traffic as the mechanism.

questions.question: Growing transformer context windows from 2,048 tokens (GPT-3) to hundreds of thousands (recent long-context models) is widely called a 'systems breakthrough' rather than merely a bigger-model story. Explain what specifically had to change to make this possible and why naive transformer attention could not simply be scaled to long context.
questions.answer: A naive attention kernel materializes an $S \times S$ score matrix for each layer and head. At $S = 100{,}000$, one FP16 head contains ten billion scores and requires about 18.6 GB under the chapter's capacity convention, before accounting for the remaining heads, layers, activations, backward-pass state, or batch. Simply adding peak FLOP/s does not remove that allocation. FlashAttention addresses the auxiliary-storage problem with tiled online softmax, computing exact dense attention without retaining the complete matrix in HBM. It still evaluates the dense scores. Sparse, local, low-rank, or other structured-attention variants instead change or approximate the interaction pattern so fewer scores are evaluated. Autoregressive serving adds a separate linearly growing KV-cache problem, managed through paging, compression, grouped-query architectures, finite windows, or offloading, each with its own trade-offs. Long context therefore required co-design across kernels, interaction patterns, and serving memory rather than one generic 'more compute' change.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why long context requires tiled attention, changed interaction patterns, or KV-cache management rather than peak-FLOP/s scaling alone.

questions.question: A recommendation system must represent 500 million unique user IDs and 100 million unique item IDs as inputs to a neural network that accepts dense vectors. Which property of embedding tables makes them the standard bridge between these high-cardinality categorical IDs and dense-network computation?
choices: Each discrete ID indexes a row of learned dense floats, so every ID becomes a trainable vector whose dimensions the downstream network can process like any other dense input — at the cost of a table whose row count equals the cardinality of the ID space.
Embeddings remove all memory accesses from inference, because once trained, the table is no longer consulted.
Embeddings convert recommendation workloads from memory-bound to compute-bound, eliminating the need for specialized memory hardware.
Embeddings are only valid in language models and are copied into RecSys without change or justification.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Embeddings are a lookup-as-representation: each ID selects a dense vector (typically 32 to 256 dimensions) from a table whose total memory is vocabulary_size * dimension * bytes_per_float. That gives the dense network something it can process while preserving learned similarity structure among IDs. The 'removes memory accesses' framing is the opposite of the truth — the lookup *is* the memory access, and it is the defining bottleneck of the DLRM architecture. The 'compute-bound' framing is wrong because the section explicitly argues RecSys becomes memory-capacity-bound. The 'only LLMs use embeddings' framing is historically wrong; embeddings predate modern LLMs and are foundational to recommendation.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why embedding tables are the canonical mechanism for converting high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors for neural-network consumption.

questions.question: A DLRM with 500 million user embeddings at 128 dimensions in FP32 already requires about 238 GB for user embeddings alone, before item embeddings or any MLP weights. Explain why the section calls DLRM 'capacity-bound' rather than compute-bound or bandwidth-bound and what that diagnosis forces on the infrastructure.
questions.answer: The defining issue is whether the model state fits before any kernel can run. The table contains 500 million rows times 128 FP32 values, or 64 billion values. At four bytes each, that is 256 billion bytes and about 238 GB under the chapter's binary capacity calculation with a visible GB label. It cannot reside on one 40-to-80 GB accelerator, so arithmetic throughput and lookup bandwidth cannot be optimized until the table has a placement plan. The system can shard it across devices, place it in a larger or slower host-memory tier, hash or compress the rows, or combine those approaches. Sharding turns a nominally local row lookup into distributed data movement and makes interconnect bandwidth and routing relevant; host placement trades capacity for access latency and bandwidth. Capacity-bound describes this first feasibility constraint, not a claim that bandwidth and compute cease to matter after placement.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why DLRM's binding constraint is memory capacity rather than compute or bandwidth, and identify embedding sharding as the required distributed-memory response.

questions.question: Why do embedding-table lookups in a production DLRM resist the cache-and-prefetch optimizations that accelerate CNN convolutions or dense MLP layers?
choices: Each request gathers a different set of embedding rows determined by the user's and items' IDs, so the access pattern is effectively random across a terabyte-scale table: hardware prefetchers cannot predict it, and caches cannot hold enough rows to exploit reuse.
Embedding tables are always smaller than the L1 cache and therefore bypass the memory hierarchy entirely.
Recommendation models do not use matrix operations anywhere, so the memory system cannot be optimized for them.
Sparse embedding access inherits the translation-equivariance properties of CNNs, which blocks caching.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Each user-and-item pair generates an ID-dependent lookup into a table large enough that no realistic cache can hold the working set, and the lookups are scattered across the table's address space with little reuse between consecutive requests. Hardware prefetchers rely on predictable sequential or strided access; random gather defeats them. The 'smaller than L1 cache' framing is reversed — the table is gigabytes to terabytes, not kilobytes. The 'no matrix operations' framing is factually wrong; DLRM contains MLPs. The translation-equivariance framing imports CNN terminology that does not describe embedding access.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why the random, ID-dependent gather pattern of embedding lookups defeats cache and prefetch optimizations designed for predictable dense-matrix access.

questions.question: Order the following high-level stages of a DLRM forward pass on one user-item example: (1) interaction layer combines dense and sparse representations, (2) bottom MLP processes continuous numerical features, (3) top MLP produces the final click-probability score, (4) embedding-table lookup retrieves vectors for categorical IDs.
questions.answer: The correct order is: (2) bottom MLP processes continuous numerical features, (4) embedding-table lookup retrieves vectors for categorical IDs, (1) interaction layer combines dense and sparse representations, (3) top MLP produces the final click-probability score. The bottom MLP and the embedding lookup operate on independent feature types and can in principle run concurrently; both must complete before the interaction layer can combine them, because the interaction explicitly consumes outputs from both. The top MLP then scores the example using the combined representation. Swapping the interaction and top MLP would score raw feature channels that have not yet been fused; swapping embeddings and interaction would try to combine vectors that do not yet exist.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the four DLRM stages and justify why the interaction layer depends on both dense and sparse inputs completing first.

questions.question: A recommendation team finds that their DLRM's combined embedding tables total 600 GB, exceeding any single 80 GB accelerator. Which distributed-memory strategy does the section identify as the required response?
choices: Shard the embedding tables across multiple accelerators so each holds a disjoint subset of rows, then use all-to-all communication at lookup time to fetch each batch's required rows from wherever they reside.
Replicate every embedding table fully on every accelerator and rely solely on data parallelism for scaling.
Replace the embedding tables with convolutions so the model becomes spatially local and fits on one device.
Move the model to a single CPU because CPUs do not have memory-capacity limits.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Sharding splits the table across devices — typical schemes partition by row (row-wise) or by embedding dimension (column-wise) — and each forward pass gathers the needed rows via an all-to-all exchange whose volume scales with batch size and embedding dimension. This is the canonical capacity-bound response. Full replication requires that every accelerator hold the full 600 GB, which is exactly the constraint sharding exists to break. Replacing embeddings with convolutions discards the categorical representation the model actually needs. The 'CPU has no limits' framing is factually wrong — host memory is also bounded, and CPU bandwidth and compute cannot serve the target request rate.
questions.learning_objective: Select embedding sharding with all-to-all communication as the capacity-bound response required when tables exceed single-accelerator memory.

questions.question: True or False: In a sharded DLRM deployment, interconnect bandwidth can become a first-order bottleneck because each GPU's forward pass may require rows from embeddings stored on many other GPUs.
questions.answer: True. Sharded embeddings induce all-to-all communication at every lookup, so bisection bandwidth on the cluster fabric determines how fast a batch's required rows can arrive. Once compute units are not the binding resource, the interconnect is — which is why recommendation systems at scale are designed around the network fabric (NVLink domains, InfiniBand, fat-tree topologies) as much as around the accelerators themselves.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why sharded embedding lookups make cluster interconnect bandwidth a first-order performance determinant in distributed recommendation systems.

questions.question: Deep plain CNNs exhibited a degradation problem in which adding layers could raise training error. Which portable architectural primitive addressed this problem and later became standard in transformers and U-Nets?
choices: Skip (residual) connections, which add an identity path from a block's input to its output so the gradient can propagate through the identity alongside the learned transformation.
Embedding tables, which replaced raw inputs with learned dense vectors and eliminated the need for deep networks.
The softmax activation applied uniformly to every hidden layer, which rescaled gradients at every depth.
Depthwise-separable convolutions, which reduced depth by factoring each layer into two cheaper operations.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The ResNet skip connection creates $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$, giving the gradient two paths backward: through the residual branch's Jacobian and through the identity. The identity term provides a direct additive path and improves conditioning when the residual Jacobian is small, which helps make networks with 50, 101, 152, and more layers trainable. It does not guarantee unattenuated gradients, because the residual term can partially cancel it. Embedding tables solve categorical representation, not depth. Softmax-everywhere is wrong on multiple counts, and depthwise-separable convolutions target efficiency rather than depth stability.
questions.learning_objective: Identify skip connections as the portable primitive that addressed the degradation problem in deep plain networks.

questions.question: Explain why the identity path in a residual block produces a well-behaved gradient in a very deep network where a plain stack of layers does not. Make the mechanism explicit, not just the empirical result.
questions.answer: In a plain deep stack, the gradient with respect to an early state traverses a product of intermediate Jacobians. Its norm is bounded above by the product of their spectral norms, so uniformly subunit norms force exponential decay; conversely, uniformly superunit minimum singular values force growth. A residual block has $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}+\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})$ and local Jacobian $\mathbf{I}+\partial\mathcal{F}/\partial\mathbf{x}$. If the residual Jacobian has spectral norm $\varepsilon<1$, the block's singular values lie between $1-\varepsilon$ and $1+\varepsilon$, keeping that local mapping near identity. This additive identity contribution gives optimization a shorter, better-conditioned route than a product-only plain stack. It is not an unconditional gradient guarantee: the residual term can partially cancel the identity direction, nonlinearities matter, and small deviations can compound across many blocks. Empirically, residual connections addressed the degradation seen in deep plain counterparts and made 50-, 101-, and 152-layer networks much easier to optimize; the mechanism later transferred to transformers and other deep architectures.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the gradient-flow mechanism of residual connections, contrasting the identity-plus-learned Jacobian chain with the product-only chain of plain deep stacks.

questions.question: A serving team is deploying a transformer that performs autoregressive generation one token at a time with an effective batch size of 1 per request. Which normalization choice is most appropriate and why?
choices: Layer normalization, because it normalizes using per-sample statistics computed across the feature dimension and is independent of batch composition, which matters when each inference request is a single sample.
Batch normalization, because it always outperforms layer normalization on GPU inference regardless of batch size.
No normalization at all, because normalization is only required during training.
Layer normalization, because it eliminates the quadratic cost of self-attention.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. LayerNorm uses each token's feature statistics, so it is independent of serving-batch composition and has the same form during training and inference. BatchNorm does not fail at inference batch size 1—evaluation uses stored running statistics—but its training activations depend on batch or batch-and-spatial statistics, creating a different operational contract that transformers generally avoid. 'BatchNorm always wins' is too strong, and removing normalization ignores its optimization role. Neither method eliminates dense attention's quadratic score computation; normalization changes feature scaling, not the interaction structure.
questions.learning_objective: Justify LayerNorm over BatchNorm for variable-batch or single-sample autoregressive serving and distinguish normalization's stabilizing role from attention's cost structure.

questions.question: Modern large language models often replace standard layer normalization with a variant that drops the mean-centering step and normalizes by the root-mean-square of the activations, saving one reduction pass and a subtraction per token. This efficient normalization variant is called ____.
questions.answer: RMSNorm (root mean square normalization). It preserves LayerNorm's per-sample, batch-independent behavior while eliminating the mean-centering pass, which reduces per-token overhead in autoregressive inference where every saved microsecond multiplies across long generations.
questions.learning_objective: Infer the RMSNorm variant from its described mechanism (drop mean-centering, normalize by RMS) and explain why the saved work matters most at inference time.

questions.question: What is the section's main argument about gating as a cross-architecture primitive?
choices: Gating is a general mechanism for selectively routing information, and variants of the same idea appear in LSTM cells, attention weights, mixture-of-experts routers, and gated linear units — making it a portable primitive rather than an LSTM-specific trick.
Gating is confined to LSTMs and has no analog in attention-based or mixture-of-experts architectures.
Gating always reduces total parameter count by a fixed factor regardless of the architecture that uses it.
Gating replaces the need for normalization layers entirely, which is why it appears in every modern architecture.
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The section's argument is that gating — computing a scalar or vector in [0, 1] that modulates a signal's pass-through — is a fundamental information-routing primitive that reappears in many disguises: LSTM's input/forget/output gates, attention's softmax weights (a learned gate over positions), MoE's expert-selection router (a learned gate over experts), and GLU-style activations in feed-forward blocks. The 'LSTM-only' framing contradicts the section's portability claim. The 'always reduces parameters' framing is a factual error. The 'replaces normalization' framing confuses two independent mechanisms.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze gating as a portable information-routing primitive whose variants span LSTMs, attention, MoE, and GLU-style activations.

questions.question: Explain why the chapter frames transformers as a *recombination* of earlier architectural building blocks rather than a complete break from prior designs, and give two concrete primitives the transformer inherits.
questions.answer: The transformer's novel idea is removing sequential recurrence in favor of parallel all-pairs attention; the rest of the architecture is borrowed. $\mathbf{Q}$, $\mathbf{K}$, and $\mathbf{V}$ projections and the output projection are dense matrix multiplications — the same GEMM primitive that MLPs and CNN 1x1 convolutions already depend on. Residual (skip) connections wrap every attention block and every feed-forward block, directly inherited from ResNet-era CNN design, and they are what make many-layer transformers trainable. Normalization (LayerNorm, later RMSNorm) also carries over from prior work, adjusted for variable-length and single-sample serving. The systems consequence is that the low-level kernel inventory developed for earlier architectures — optimized GEMM libraries, fused residual-plus-norm kernels, mixed-precision execution paths — transfers directly to transformers, which is why hardware designed for dense linear algebra was ready to execute them the moment they appeared.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze transformers as a recombination of inherited primitives (dense GEMM, skip connections, normalization) around the novel self-attention core and explain why earlier kernel and hardware work transferred.
